slides.narration: Welcome. Today we study Madam Rides the Bus, a story by the Tamil writer Vallikkannan about a village girl who secretly plans her first bus ride. Please read the story itself in your textbook, First Flight. This lesson does not repeat it. Instead we will follow Valli's adventure, understand her character, and see how a happy outing becomes a lesson about life and death.

Use these slides for the sequence, Valli's character and the themes.
Explain events **in your own words**; report what characters say instead of quoting it.
Practise the extract questions, which use SOYL commentary on the story.

It is told in the third person, but the narrator stays very close to Valli, so we share her thoughts and feelings. It is set in a village, on the bus road, and in the nearest town.

slides.narration: The story moves in seven stages. Valli dreams of the bus from her doorway. She researches and saves. She boards the bus and is nicknamed madam. The outward ride is pure joy. She sees the town from her seat. On the way back she sees something that saddens her. And she comes home carrying a secret. Keep this map in mind.

slides.heading: Summary 1: the dream and the plan
slides.body_md: Valli, an eight-year-old village girl with nobody her age to play with, spends her time watching the street from her front door. The bus to the nearest town fascinates her. She quietly listens to people who use it, asks a few careful questions, and learns the distance, the time and the fare. She saves every coin, resisting the treats of the village fair, and picks the time of her mother's afternoon nap for her secret trip.
slides.narration: Valli is eight, and her entertainment is the view from her front door. The bus that runs to the nearest town fascinates her. So she makes a plan. She listens to people who use the bus, asks a few careful questions, and learns everything she needs. Then she saves every coin, even when the village fair tempts her, and chooses her mother's afternoon nap as the time to go.

slides.heading: Summary 2: boarding the bus
slides.body_md: At the bus stop Valli refuses the conductor's help and climbs in by herself. Amused by her grown-up manner, he addresses her with mock respect as madam, the word in the title. She pays her fare and takes her seat with great seriousness. An elderly woman passenger fusses over her, and Valli, who wants to be treated as a proper traveller, keeps her replies short.
slides.narration: At the bus stop, Valli refuses the conductor's help and climbs in on her own. He is amused by her serious, grown-up manner and starts to call her madam, with mock respect. That is where the title comes from. She pays her own fare. When an elderly woman fusses over her, Valli is irritated. She wants to be treated as a passenger, not as a little child.

slides.heading: Check: the order of events
slides.narration: Your turn. Six events from Valli's adventure are shuffled. Put them in the order in which they happen, from the doorway to the road home.

slides.heading: Summary 3: the outward ride
slides.body_md: On the way to the town Valli is enchanted by everything she sees through the window. A young cow is trapped on the road ahead of the bus, and the horn only frightens it into running harder; Valli is helpless with laughter.
slides.narration: On the way to the town, Valli is enchanted. Trees, water and distant hills pass the window, and each sight is a wonder. Then a young cow gets stuck on the road ahead of the bus. The horn only frightens it into running harder, and Valli laughs and laughs. Remember this cow. The writer will bring it back.

slides.heading: Summary 4: the town
slides.body_md: At the town Valli does not get off. She had planned a ride, not a visit, and must be home before her mother wakes, so she buys a ticket for the return journey and watches the busy town from her seat. The conductor, now fond of her, offers to buy her a drink; she politely refuses.
slides.narration: When the bus reaches the town, Valli surprises the conductor by staying in her seat. Her plan was a ride, not a visit, and she must be home before her mother wakes. So she buys a return ticket and watches the town through the window. The conductor, who now likes her, offers her a drink. She politely says no.

slides.heading: Summary 5: the return and home
slides.body_md: On the way back Valli sees the same young cow lying dead by the road, killed by a passing vehicle. Her joy disappears and the view loses all its charm. She reaches home safely, and the trip remains her own secret.
slides.narration: On the way back, Valli sees the same young cow lying dead beside the road. A passing vehicle has killed it. Her happiness disappears, and she turns away from the window. She reaches home safely, and nobody learns about her journey. But she is not quite the same girl who set out. She has had her first real meeting with death.

slides.narration: The heart of the story is a contrast. On the way out, the cow is alive and funny, the view is wonderful, and Valli is proud and happy. On the way back, the same road brings the dead cow, and Valli falls silent. The same journey holds both joy and sorrow. That is the lesson about life and death she learns without any adult explaining it.

slides.narration: Around that contrast sit other themes. Curiosity, which starts the whole adventure. Planning and determination, in her research and saving. Independence and self-respect, in the way she refuses help and fussing. Life and death, through the cow. Growing up, because she returns a little older in mind. And the gap between children and adults, who either tease or fuss.

slides.narration: Let us sketch Valli. She is curious and a resourceful planner. She is self-controlled, saving every coin. She is independent and proud, refusing help and favours. She is observant and full of joy on the outward ride. And she is sensitive, as the dead cow shows. In answers, always pair a trait with a moment from the story.

slides.narration: The adults help us see Valli more clearly. The conductor is good-humoured and kind; his teasing turns into fondness. The elderly woman is fussy and treats Valli as helpless, which Valli resents. Her mother naps through the whole adventure. Each adult underestimates her, and each time Valli shows that she can manage on her own.

slides.heading: Was Valli right to go alone?
columns:
**Yes: admirable independence**

- she planned carefully and paid her own way
- she behaved sensibly among strangers
- she gained knowledge no lesson could teach

**No: a real risk**

- an eight-year-old travelling secretly could be lost or hurt
- her mother would not know where to look
- true independence includes judging safety
slides.narration: A common long question asks whether Valli was right to travel alone and in secret. One side praises her careful planning, her sensible behaviour and what she learnt. The other side points out the danger to a small child and her mother's ignorance of where she was. The best answers take a stand and still show they understand the other side.

slides.heading: Style and narrative technique
bullets: **Third-person narration close to Valli:** we see the world through a child's eyes.
**Gentle humour:** a small girl behaving like an important adult passenger.
**Contrast:** the outward and return journeys mirror each other.
**Foreshadowing:** the running cow prepares for the dead cow.
**Simple, vivid description** of village, road and town.
slides.narration: How is the story told? A third-person narrator stays close to Valli, so we see the world through a child's eyes. Gentle humour comes from a little girl behaving like an important passenger. The two journeys are built as a contrast. The running cow is an example of foreshadowing, because it prepares us for what comes later. And the descriptions are simple and vivid.

slides.heading: Contrast and foreshadowing: SOYL's own examples
slides.body_md: Practise the two devices that shape this story. These sentences are SOYL's own, not from the story:
bullets: *In the morning the kite danced above the rooftops; by evening its torn string hung from a wire.* — contrast between two moments
*Ravi waved cheerfully at the old boat tied by the river, not knowing he would need it that night.* — foreshadowing
*The same street that echoed with the wedding band at noon was silent at midnight.* — contrast of place and mood
slides.narration: Here are three sentences of our own. A kite dances in the morning and hangs torn by evening: a contrast between two moments. Ravi waves at an old boat he will need that night: foreshadowing, because an early detail prepares for a later event. A street loud at noon and silent at midnight: contrast of mood. Now find the same devices in Valli's two journeys.

slides.narration: These words will help you write about the story. A pastime is something you do for fun. The fare is the money paid for a journey, and the conductor sells tickets. A temptation is a strong wish to do something you should not. Dignity is a calm, serious manner. Mock respect is pretend respect, used as a joke. And mature means grown-up in thinking.

**Points + evidence:** researches and saves like an adult; insists on being treated as an equal passenger; keeps to her plan in the town.
**Qualification:** her laughter and her shock at the cow show she is still a child.
**Link + conclusion:** the trip moves her a step towards real maturity.

sections.heading: 3. Themes and message
sections.body_md:
- **Curiosity:** the wish to see the world beyond home.
- **Planning and determination:** research, saving and timing.
- **Independence and self-respect:** refusing help, favours and fussing.
- **Life and death:** the cow, alive and then dead.
- **Growing up:** a child returns a little wiser.
- **Childhood and the adult world:** adults tease or fuss; Valli insists on equality.

**Message:** growing up means discovering both the wonders and the sorrows of the world, often in the same day.

questions.passage_md: Valli's world at the start of the story is the view from her front door. With nobody her age nearby to play with, the life of the street is her chief entertainment, and the most exciting thing in it is the bus that runs between her village and the nearest town. Each time it passes, full of travellers going somewhere she has never been, her longing grows. What makes Valli remarkable is that she does not stop at longing. Wishing is what most children do; Valli, at eight, turns her wish into a project with a budget and a timetable.

questions.stem_md: Imagine you are the bus conductor. Describe your small passenger to a friend that evening, in 100–120 words.
questions.solution_md: Conversational account in the first person. Content consistent with the story: her age and independence, refusal of help, the nickname, staying on the bus, refusal of the drink, her silence on the way back. Tone warm and amused.

answer.model_answer_md: You will not believe the passenger I had today. She was a tiny girl, no older than eight, travelling all by herself. When I offered to help her up the step, she refused and climbed in on her own, as proud as a queen. I could not resist calling her madam. She paid her fare, sat up straight and stared at the view as if she owned the road. When the bus reached the town, she would not get off; she simply bought another ticket for the return ride. I offered her a cold drink, but she turned it down politely. On the way back she went very quiet. I hope she reached home safely.

questions.stem_md: Valli travelled alone and in secret. Should children be encouraged to be as independent as Valli? Give your view in 100–120 words.
questions.solution_md: A clear stand + what Valli’s independence shows (planning, saving, dignity) + the risks of secrecy + a balanced conclusion. A reasoned stronger view either way can also earn full marks.

answer.model_answer_md: Independence is valuable, and Valli shows its best side. She researched her trip, saved her money, resisted temptation and behaved with dignity among strangers. These are habits every child should build. However, her secrecy was risky. An eight-year-old travelling alone could have been lost, hurt or misled, and her mother would not even have known where to look. True independence includes good judgement about safety. In my view, children should be encouraged to plan, take decisions and try new experiences, but with a trusted adult informed. Valli’s story celebrates a brave, capable child, but it also quietly reminds us that the world beyond the doorway contains real dangers.

questions.stem_md: Valli refuses to be treated as a child by the adults she meets. Discuss how she deals with each of them, in 100–120 words.
questions.solution_md: Valli’s dealings with the conductor (help, nickname, drink), the elderly woman (fussing) and her mother (secret) + what they reveal (self-respect, desire to grow up).

answer.model_answer_md: Valli insists on being treated as an equal throughout her journey. With the conductor, she refuses help to climb in and does not laugh at his teasing nickname, though by the end she has won his affection. With the elderly woman passenger, who fusses over a girl travelling alone, she keeps her replies short and cool, resenting the suggestion that she cannot look after herself. In the town she turns down the conductor’s offer of a drink, unwilling to accept favours. Even with her own mother she keeps her plan secret, sure she can manage alone. Her firmness is sometimes funny, but it shows real self-respect and a strong wish to grow up.

questions.stem_md: What is the importance of the young cow in *Madam Rides the Bus*? Answer in 100–120 words.
questions.solution_md: The cow in both journeys + what it represents (joy, life) + the contrast and its effect on Valli + its role in the story’s meaning.

answer.model_answer_md: The young cow appears only twice, yet it carries the story’s deepest meaning. On the outward journey it races ahead of the bus, and Valli laughs at it helplessly. It stands for the playful, carefree spirit of the day and of Valli herself. On the return journey the same animal lies dead by the roadside. The contrast is sudden and painful, and Valli’s delight in the view disappears. Through the cow, the writer shows that life is fragile and that joy and sorrow can follow each other within hours. Without the cow, the story would be a pleasant outing; with it, the ride becomes Valli’s first step towards understanding life.
